first_reader_source: PDF PDFs/Alcohol/Schuckit_2014_WithdrawalDelirium.pdf: the version of record, N Engl J Med 2014;371(22):2109–2113
title: Recognition and management of withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens)

claims.statement: In people in alcohol withdrawal, withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens) is defined in DSM-5, as a narrative review sets it out (Schuckit, 2014; no funding statement, no conflicts reported), as alcohol withdrawal after stopping or cutting down heavy, prolonged drinking (at least two of eight signs: an overactive nervous system, hand tremor, sleeplessness, nausea or vomiting, brief hallucinations or illusions, agitation, anxiety, seizures) together with delirium, a disturbance of attention, awareness and thinking that comes on quickly and fluctuates. The review relays, second-hand and without the designs or settings of its sources, that about half of people with alcohol use disorder have withdrawal symptoms when they cut down or stop and that seizures, delirium or both develop in 3 to 5 in 100 of them; that 3 to 5 in 100 patients in hospital for alcohol withdrawal meet the criteria for withdrawal delirium; that it usually begins about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms appear and lasts from 1 to 8 days or more, usually 2 or 3; and that about 1 to 4 in 100 hospital patients with withdrawal delirium die, usually from overheating, heart rhythm disturbances, complications of seizures or other illnesses, a rate the author says timely diagnosis and treatment could lower. It names, as signs that delirium is more likely, a high withdrawal score (above 15 on the CIWA-Ar scale, especially with a systolic blood pressure above 150 mm Hg or a pulse above 100 a minute), recent withdrawal seizures (seen in 20 in 100 people with delirium), earlier delirium or seizures, older age, recent use of other depressant drugs, and other medical problems such as low potassium or magnesium. In the placebo groups of four small trials from 1961 to 1980, pooled in a 1997 review, 11 of 186 people in withdrawal, about 6 in 100, developed delirium (editors' sum; Mayo-Smith, 1997; a practice guideline of a US medical society, ASAM, with no funding or conflict statement). The trials' definitions predate DSM-IV and the review does not describe their settings, the narrative review's figures are second-hand, and none of these sources measures how often delirium happens to people who stop drinking outside hospital. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Schuckit 2014 (second-hand, sources' designs and settings not given): withdrawal symptoms in about 50% of people with alcohol use disorder who cut down or stop, seizures, delirium or both in 3 to 5% of them; withdrawal delirium in 3 to 5% of patients hospitalized for withdrawal; onset about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms, duration 1 to 8 days or more (usually 2 or 3); case fatality about 1 to 4% of hospitalized patients with withdrawal delirium; recent withdrawal seizures in 20% of people with delirium. Mayo-Smith 1997, Table 2, placebo groups: delirium 2 of 30, 1 of 11, 8 of 130 and 0 of 15 (trials of 1961, 1965, 1969 and 1980); 11 of 186, 5.9% (editors' sum).

claims.statement: In people in alcohol withdrawal in placebo-controlled trials published from 1961 to 1983 (most of them of chlordiazepoxide; those in the Cochrane review all randomized), benzodiazepines compared with placebo reduced withdrawal seizures: in a Cochrane review searched to December 2009, 1 of 149 people given a benzodiazepine against 14 of 175 given placebo had a seizure in three trials (risk ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.69), about 1 against 8 in 100 in the review's illustration (13 against 80 per 1,000), graded moderate quality by the review (Amato et al., 2010; funded by a Rome health authority and the Italian medicines agency; no conflicts declared). An earlier review found 7.7 fewer seizures per 100 people treated (95% CI 3.5 to 12.0 fewer; five trials) and 4.9 fewer cases of delirium per 100 (0.7 to 9.0 fewer; four trials, 3 of 172 against 11 of 186 people, editors' sums) (Mayo-Smith, 1997; a practice guideline of a US medical society, ASAM, with no funding or conflict statement). The two reviews share three trials, and one trial from 1969 supplies most of the events, so they are not independent confirmation. Against other medicines pooled together (trials up to 2009; anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, clonidine, beta-blockers and others), benzodiazepines showed no clear difference in seizures (risk ratio 0.52, 0.21 to 1.31; 12 trials) or delirium (0.65, 0.21 to 1.98; 8 trials); against anticonvulsants alone the estimates leaned towards the anticonvulsants, also without a clear difference (seizures 1.70, 0.39 to 7.37; delirium 1.90, 0.43 to 8.38), and adverse events tended to be more frequent with benzodiazepines (1.31, 0.99 to 1.72). Phenothiazine antipsychotics given alone did not reduce delirium compared with placebo (risk difference 0.0 per 100, −5.8 to +6.6) and were followed by more seizures (11.4 more per 100, 6.2 to 16.6) and more delirium (6.6 more per 100, 2.4 to 10.8) than benzodiazepines or paraldehyde. In the comparisons with other medicines, deaths occurred in 4 of the 32 trials in the mortality analysis. For people already in withdrawal delirium, a narrative review describes the treatment evidence as nine controlled trials from 1959 to 1978 and later uncontrolled studies (Schuckit, 2014). Most trials did not report how allocation was concealed, events were few, outcome definitions predate DSM-IV, and people with serious liver, heart, lung or kidney disease or other drug dependence were usually left out. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Amato et al. 2010 (Cochrane, search to December 2009): against placebo, seizures RR 0.16 (0.04 to 0.69), 3 trials, 324 participants, 1/149 against 14/175, I² 0%, GRADE moderate, illustrative 80 against 13 per 1000 (3 to 55); against other drugs, seizures RR 0.52 (0.21 to 1.31), 12 trials, 1228, 5/442 against 37/786; against anticonvulsants 1.70 (0.39 to 7.37), 7 trials, 523; delirium RR 0.65 (0.21 to 1.98), 8 trials, 893, I² 52%; against anticonvulsants 1.90 (0.43 to 8.38), 5 trials, 342; at least one adverse event RR 1.31 (0.99 to 1.72), 18 trials, 919, GRADE low; deaths in 4 of the 32 trials of the mortality analysis (2 with benzodiazepines, 5 with other drugs, editors' sum). Mayo-Smith 1997: risk difference, benzodiazepine against placebo, delirium −4.9 per 100 (−9.0 to −0.7), 4 trials, 3/172 against 11/186; seizures −7.7 per 100 (−12.0 to −3.5), 5 trials, 1/182 against 17/196 (editors' sums from Table 2); phenothiazine against placebo, delirium 0.0 (−5.8 to +6.6), seizures +4.6 (−2.6 to +11.9); phenothiazine against benzodiazepine or paraldehyde, delirium +6.6 (+2.4 to +10.8), seizures +11.4 (+6.2 to +16.6).
